subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: Intellectual Courage: Following Evidence Where It Leads
description: A quick win: understand Intellectual Courage: Following Evidence Where It Leads.

hook.text: Barry Marshall drank a petri dish of bacteria to prove ulcers were caused by infection, not stress. He was right.

buildup.text: Intellectual courage: following evidence to its conclusion, even when that conclusion is unpopular, uncomfortable, or.

discovery.text: Ignaz Semmelweis proved handwashing prevented deaths in 1847. Doctors rejected him. He died in an asylum. He was right.

twist.text: It's not just scientists. Everyday intellectual courage means changing your mind publicly when the evidence demands it.

climax.text: The hardest evidence to follow is evidence against your own identity.

punchline.text: The truth doesn't care about your comfort. Follow it anyway.

quiz.question: What is intellectual courage?
options: Following evidence to its conclusion even when it's uncomfortable

details.summary: Intellectual courage is the willingness to follow evidence to conclusions that are unpopular, uncomfortable, or personally costly. It means changing your mind publicly when the evidence demands it.
details.whyItMatters: Without intellectual courage, evidence-based thinking is hollow. The hardest part is not gathering evidence but accepting what it tells you.
takeaways: Intellectual courage means accepting uncomfortable conclusions
It requires willingness to be wrong publicly
Social pressure is the greatest enemy of evidence-following

faq.question: What is a historical example of intellectual courage in science?
faq.answer: Galileo defended heliocentrism despite church opposition. Ignaz Semmelweis advocated handwashing in hospitals despite ridicule from colleagues. Both followed evidence to unpopular conclusions at great personal cost.

faq.question: How can you build intellectual courage in everyday situations?
faq.answer: Start by changing your mind publicly on small matters. Celebrate when you discover you were wrong because it means you learned something. Over time, this builds the habit of following evidence even when it is socially uncomfortable.
